In practice, the constant assumption can approximately hold for some time, in which the second term in Eq. 9 goes to zero exponentially and the stable rank of Gt goes down, yielding low-rank gradient Gt. The final stable rank is de- termined by sr(G∥ t0 ), which is estimated to be low-rank by the following: Corollary 3.4 (Low-rank Gt). If the gradient takes the parametric form Gt = 1 N PN i=1(ai −BiWtfi)f⊤ i with all Bi full-rank, and N′ := rank({fi}) < n, then sr(G∥ t0 ) ≤ n − N′ and thus sr(Gt) ≤ n/2 for large t. Remarks. The gradient form is justified by Theorem 3.2. Intuitively, when N′ is small, Gt is a summation of N′ rank-1 update and is naturally low rank; on the other hand, when N′ becomes larger and closer to n, then the training dynamics has smaller null space V1, which also makes Gt low-rank. The full-rank assumption of {Bi} is reasonable, e.g., in LLMs, the output dimensions of the networks (i.e., the vocabulary size) is often huge compared to matrix di- mensions. In general if the batch size N is large, then it becomes a bit tricky to characterize the minimal eigenspace V1 of S. On the other hand, if V1 has nice structure, then sr(Gt) can be bounded even further: Corollary 3.5 (Low-rank Gt with special structure of V1). If V1(S) is 1-dimensional with decomposable eigenvector v = y ⊗z, then sr(G∥ t0 ) = 1 and thus Gt becomes rank-1. One rare failure case of Lemma 3.3 is whenG∥ t0 is precisely zero, in whichsr(G∥ t0 ) becomes undefined. This happens to be true if t0 = 0, i.e., Ai, Bi and Ci are constant through- out the entire training process. Fortunately, for practical training, this does not happen. Transformers. For Transformers, we can also separately prove that the weight gradient of the lower layer (i.e., project-up) weight of feed forward network (FFN) becomes low rank over time, using the JoMA framework (Tian et al., 2024). Gradient Low-rank Projection (GaLore) Since the gradient G may have a low-rank structure, if we can keep the gradient statistics of a small “core” of gradient G in optimizer states, rather than G itself, then the memory consumption can be reduced substantially. This leads to our proposed GaLore strategy: Definition 3.6 (Gradient Low-rank Projection ( GaLore)). Gradient low-rank projection (GaLore) denotes the follow- ing gradient update rules (η is the learning rate): WT = W0 + η T−1X t=0 ˜Gt, ˜Gt = Ptρt(P⊤ t GtQt)Q⊤ t (10) where Pt ∈ Rm×r and Qt ∈ Rn×r are projection matrices. Different from LoRA, GaLore explicitly utilizes the low- rank updates instead of introducing additional low-rank adaptors and hence does not alter the training dynamics. In the following, we show that GaLore converges under a similar (but more general) form of gradient update rule (Eqn. 8). This form corresponds to Eqn. 6 but with a larger batch size. GaLore for Memory-Efficient Training For a complex optimization problem such as LLM pre- training, it may be difficult to capture the entire gradient trajectory with a single low-rank subspace. One reason is that the principal subspaces ofBt and Ct (and thus Gt) may change over time. In fact, if we keep the same projection P and Q, then the learned weights will only grow along these subspaces, which is not longer full-parameter train- ing. Fortunately, for this, GaLore can switch subspaces during training and learn full-rank weights without increas- ing the memory footprint. In the experiment section, we show that allowing multiple low-rank subspaces is the key to achieving the successful pre-training of LLMs. Following the above procedure, the switching frequency T becomes a hyperparameter. The ablation study (Fig. 5) shows a sweet spot exists. A very frequent subspace change increases the overhead (since new Pt and Qt need to be computed) and breaks the condition of constant projection in Theorem 3.8. In practice, it may also impact the fidelity of the optimizer states, which accumulate over multiple training steps. On the other hand, a less frequent change may make the algorithm stuck into a region that is no longer important to optimize (convergence proof in Theorem 3.8 only means good progress in the designated subspace, but does not mean good overall performance). While optimal T depends on the total training iterations and task com- plexity, we find that a value between T = 50 to T = 1000 makes no much difference. Thus, the total computational overhead induced by SVD is negligible (< 10%) compared to other memory-efficient training techniques such as mem- ory offloading (Rajbhandari et al., 2020). 4.2. Combining with Existing Techniques GaLore is compatible with existing memory-efficient opti- mization techniques. In our work, we mainly consider ap- plying GaLore with 8-bit optimizers and per-layer weight updates. 8-bit optimizers. Dettmers et al. (2022) proposed 8-bit Adam optimizer that maintains 32-bit optimizer perfor- mance at a fraction of the memory footprint. We apply Ga- Lore directly to the existing implementation of 8-bit Adam. Per-layer weight updates. In practice, the optimizer typ- ically performs a single weight update for all layers after backpropagation. This is done by storing the entire weight gradients in memory. To further reduce the memory foot- print during training, we adopt per-layer weight updates to GaLore, which performs the weight updates during back- propagation. This is the same technique proposed in recent works to reduce memory requirement (Lv et al., 2023a;b). 4.4. Hyperparameters of GaLore In addition to Adam’s original hyperparameters, GaLore only introduces very few additional hyperparameters: the rank r which is also present in LoRA, the subspace change frequency T (see Sec. 4.1), and the scale factor α. Scale factor α controls the strength of the low-rank update, which is similar to the scale factor α/r appended to the low-rank adaptor in Hu et al. (2022). We note that the α does not depend on the rank r in our case. This is because, when r is small during pre-training, α/r significantly af- fects the convergence rate, unlike fine-tuning. 5. We note that our results do not require offloading strategies or checkpointing, which can significantly impact training throughput. We leave optimizing the efficiency of GaLore implementation for future work. 6. Ablation Study How many subspaces are needed during pre-training? We observe that both too frequent and too slow changes of subspaces hurt the convergence, as shown in Fig. 5 (left). The reason has been discussed in Sec. 4.1. In general, for small r, the subspace switching should happen more to avoid wasting optimization steps in the wrong subspace, while for large r the gradient updates cover more sub- spaces, providing more cushion. How does the rank of subspace affect the convergence? Within a certain range of rank values, decreasing the rank only slightly affects the convergence rate, causing a slow- down with a nearly linear trend. As shown in Fig. 5 (right), training with a rank of 128 using 80K steps achieves a lower loss than training with a rank of 512 using 20K steps. Figure 5: Ablation study of GaLore on 130M models. Left: varying subspace update frequency T. Right: varying subspace rank and training iterations. This shows that GaLore can be used to trade-off between memory and computational cost. In a memory-constrained scenario, reducing the rank allows us to stay within the memory budget while training for more steps to preserve the performance. 7. Conclusion We propose GaLore, a memory-efficient pre-training and fine-tuning strategy for large language models. GaLore sig- nificantly reduces memory usage by up to 65.5% in opti- mizer states while maintaining both efficiency and perfor- mance for large-scale LLM pre-training and fine-tuning. We identify several open problems for GaLore, which in- clude (1) applying GaLore on training of various mod- els such as vision transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020), (2) further enhanc- ing memory efficiency by employing low-memory projec- tion matrices, and (3) exploring the feasibility of elastic data distributed training on low-bandwidth consumer-grade hardware. We hope that our work will inspire future research on memory-efficient training from the perspective of gradi- ent low-rank projection. We believe that GaLore will be a valuable tool for the community, enabling the training of large-scale models on consumer-grade hardware with lim- ited resources. 9GaLore: Memory-Efficient LLM Training by Gradient Low-Rank Projection Impact Statement This paper aims to improve the memory efficiency of train- ing LLMs in order to reduce the environmental impact of LLM pre-training and fine-tuning. Additional Related Works Adafactor (Shazeer & Stern, 2018) achieves sub-linear memory cost by factorizing the second-order statistics by a row- column outer product. GaLore shares similarities with Adafactor in terms of utilizing low-rank factorization to reduce memory cost, but GaLore focuses on the low-rank structure of the gradients, while Adafactor focuses on the low-rank structure of the second-order statistics. GaLore can reduce the memory cost for both first-order and second-order statistics, and can be combined with Adafactor to achieve further memory reduction. In contrast to the previous memory-efficient optimization methods, GaLore operates independently as the optimizers directly receive the low-rank gradients without knowing their full-rank counterparts. The fused backward operation proposed by LOMO (Lv et al., 2023b) mitigates the memory cost of storing weight gradients during training. Integrated with the standard SGD optimizer, LOMO achieves zero optimizer and gradient memory cost during training. AdaLOMO (Lv et al., 2023a) enhances this approach by combining the fused backward operation with adaptive learning rate for each parameter, similarly achieving minimal optimizer memory cost. While LOMO and AdaLOMO represent significant advancements in memory-efficient optimization for fine-tuning or continual pre-training, they might not be directly applicable to pre-training from scratch at larger scales. For example, the vanilla Adafactor, adopted by AdaLOMO, has been demonstrated to lead to increased training instabilities at larger scales (Rae et al., 2021; Chowdhery et al., 2023; Wortsman et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2022). We believe integrating GaLore with the fused backward operation may offer a promising avenue for achieving memory-efficient large-scale pre-training from scratch. B. Proofs B.1. Reversibility Definition B.1 (Reversiblity (Tian et al., 2020)) . A network N that maps input x to output y = N(x) is reversible, if there exists L(x; W) so that y = L(x; W)x, and the backpropagated gradient gx satisfies gx = L⊤(x; W)gy, where gy is the backpropagated gradient at the output y. Here L(x; W) depends on the input x and weight W in the network N. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper addresses significant memory challenges in Large Language Model (LLM) training due to growing weights and optimizer states, proposing Gradient Low-Rank Projection (GaLore). GaLore is a training strategy that enables full-parameter learning while being more memory-efficient than common low-rank adaptation methods like LoRA. The core contribution is leveraging the slow-changing low-rank structure of the gradient matrix, rather than approximating the weight matrix itself as low-rank. GaLore significantly reduces memory usage by up to 65.5% in optimizer states and 63.3% total training memory (with 8-bit GaLore), while maintaining comparable performance for pre-training LLaMA 1B and 7B models on C4, and fine-tuning RoBERTa on GLUE tasks. Notably, it demonstrates the feasibility of pre-training a 7B model on consumer GPUs with 24GB memory (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090) without requiring model parallelism, checkpointing, or offloading. GaLore is optimizer-agnostic and simple to integrate.
llm_extracted_info.methodology: GaLore operates by computing two projection matrices, P and Q, to project the high-dimensional gradient matrix G into a compact low-rank form (P⊤GQ). This low-rank representation is then used for gradient updates, substantially reducing the memory cost of optimizer states. To allow for full-parameter learning and adapt to changing gradient subspaces, GaLore permits switching across low-rank subspaces during training; P and Q are re-initialized periodically (e.g., every 200 iterations) by performing Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on the current gradient. The approach is compatible with existing memory-efficient techniques, such as 8-bit optimizers (e.g., 8-bit Adam) and per-layer weight updates. The paper provides theoretical justification for the low-rank property of gradients during training, specifically for reversible networks and lower-layer FFN weights in Transformers, and offers a convergence analysis for GaLore.
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: GaLore was evaluated on both LLM pre-training and fine-tuning tasks. For pre-training, LLaMA-based architectures (60M, 130M, 350M, 1B, and 7B parameters) were trained on the C4 dataset (up to 19.7B tokens) using BF16 format. Experiments involved tuning learning rates for various methods (Full-Rank, Low-Rank, LoRA, ReLoRA) using Adam, AdamW, 8-bit Adam, and Adafactor optimizers. Memory measurements were conducted on a single device without activation checkpointing or offloading. The LLaMA 7B pre-training used an 8-node setup with 64 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. For fine-tuning, RoBERTa-Base models were fine-tuned on GLUE tasks, BERT-Base on SQuAD, and Gemma-2b, Phi-2, and LLaMA-7B on OpenAssistant Conversations and Belle-1M datasets. Evaluation metrics included validation perplexity for pre-training, average scores and per-task metrics for GLUE, Exact Match and F1 scores for SQuAD, and testing perplexity for OpenAssistant and Belle-1M. Feasibility on consumer-grade hardware was demonstrated using an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB memory).
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The current implementation of 8-bit GaLore exhibits a throughput overhead of 17% compared to 8-bit Adam, suggesting room for optimization. The frequency of subspace changes (hyperparameter T) presents a trade-off: too frequent changes increase SVD computational overhead and can break convergence conditions, while infrequent changes may hinder optimization progress. The theoretical analyses for gradient low-rankness rely on assumptions such as constant parameters (Ai, Bi, Ci) for a period, full-rank Bi, and for Transformers, fixed and column-orthonormal embedding matrices, linear activation functions, and stationary backpropagated gradients. A theoretical edge case exists where the gradient projection onto the minimal eigenspace could be precisely zero, making stable rank undefined, though this is stated not to occur in practical training.
llm_extracted_info.future_research_directions: Future research directions include extending GaLore's application to other model architectures, such as vision transformers and diffusion models. Further enhancements in memory efficiency could be achieved by employing low-memory projection matrices (e.g., through quantization or efficient parameterization). The authors also suggest exploring the feasibility of elastic data distributed training on low-bandwidth consumer-grade hardware. Optimizing the efficiency of GaLore's implementation to reduce throughput overhead is also a key area. Additionally, integrating GaLore with fused backward operations like those in LOMO/AdaLOMO is identified as a promising avenue, and further theoretical analysis for architectures like self-attention using frameworks like JoMA is mentioned.

new_method.method:
Open Problems: Existing gradient-projection methods such as GaLore drastically reduce optimizer-state memory, but three obstacles prevent their direct adoption for large-scale scientific ML (SciML):
1. Costly full-matrix SVD: every 100–200 steps the gradient of each large parameter matrix must be decomposed, creating a non-negligible wall-clock overhead that grows quadratically with hidden size.
2. Physics-ignorant sub-spaces: the purely data-driven sub-spaces chosen by vanilla GaLore ignore known symmetries (e.g. rotational, permutation, temporal causality) that are crucial for PINNs, neural operators and molecular transformers, so low-rank projection can inadvertently discard gradient directions needed to preserve physical constraints.
3. Lack of cross-task generality: current evaluations focus on language modelling; it is unknown whether low-rank gradients persist in stiff PDE regimes or in long-range molecular interactions, and whether memory savings can be realised on 1–1.5 B parameter SciML transformers within <48 GB GPU budgets.
Resolving these issues would enable full-parameter optimisation of billion-scale SciML models on single or few consumer GPUs, accelerating research in CFD, climate modelling and drug discovery.
Methods: We propose Physically-Aware Hierarchical GaLore (Phi-GaLore): a symmetry-aware, two-stage gradient projection framework.
Stage-1: Fast hierarchical randomised projection
• For every weight matrix W∈ℝ^{m×n}, compute a fast Randomised Subspace Sketch G̃=P_rᵀ G Q_r with r≈32 using one pass of Count-Sketch (no SVD) every iteration – O((m+n)r) time, negligible memory.
• Maintain exponentially-moving-average (EMA) of this sketch to damp stochastic noise.
Stage-2: Physics-informed sub-space refinement (every T≈400 steps)
• Build a small r×r covariance C=G̃ G̃ᵀ; perform SVD on C only (cost O(r³)).
• Augment the left singular vectors with analytic symmetry bases B (e.g. divergence-free basis for incompressible flow, SO(3) spherical-harmonic basis for molecular rotations).  Final projector P=[U_r  B] is orthonormalised by two iterations of Gram–Schmidt.
Hierarchical sharing
• For groups of layers that share resolution (e.g. all attention value matrices at level k) use a common projector; this shrinks SVD count by >8×.
Optimizer integration
• Implement in PyTorch/JAX as a drop-in optax/torch.optim wrapper that keeps EMA sketch and symmetry bases in BF16.
• Compatible with 8-bit Adam states and FLORA-style momentum compression; choose the cheaper of Phi-GaLore and FLORA on a layer-by-layer basis.
Differences to prior work
• Replaces expensive full-gradient SVD with tiny r×r SVD plus Count-Sketch.
• Injects task-specific symmetry bases, guaranteeing invariance/equivariance of projected gradients.
• Introduces cross-layer projector sharing to amortise cost on deep transformers.
• Targets SciML workloads rather than NLP.
Experimental Setup: Models
1. PINNsFormer-Large (≈1 B params) for transient 2-D Navier–Stokes, 1024 pseudo-sequence length.
2. Transolver-XL (≈1.3 B params) for 3-D AirfRANS industrial benchmark.
3. GeoMFormer-Base (≈1 B) fine-tuned on MolPuzzle (217 molecules) for HOMO-LUMO gap prediction.
Baselines
• Full-rank AdamW (mixed precision).
• LoRA (rank-64) fine-tuning.
• Original GaLore (rank-64, T=200).
• FLORA (rank-64, τ=64) where applicable.
Metrics
• Physics tasks: relative L2 error on velocity/pressure fields, volume-averaged residual, inference stability under mesh refinement.
• Molecular task: MAE on HOMO-LUMO, Spearman-ρ.
• Computational: peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, training tokens/s (or grid-points/s), total wall-clock to reach a fixed error, projection overhead %.
Protocols
• Train each model for a fixed 150K gradient steps on 2×RTX 4090 (24 GB) or 1×A100-80 GB.
• Ablate (r∈{16,32,64}, presence/absence of symmetry bases, projector sharing factor).
• Robustness: (a) noisy boundary conditions, (b) random mesh perturbations, (c) molecular conformer noise.
• Measure rank of true gradients during training to validate low-rank assumption in SciML.
Result: Expected outcomes:
• Phi-GaLore matches or beats full-rank accuracy (≤1% degradation) on all tasks.
• Reduces optimizer-state memory by 60–68 % vs full-rank and by 10–15 % vs GaLore through projector sharing; fits 1.3 B model in 24 GB.
• Cuts projection overhead from GaLore’s 14–20 % to <5 %; overall training throughput +18 % vs GaLore, +2 % vs Full-rank despite memory gain.
• Symmetry bases lower Navier–Stokes rL2 error by ~8 % relative to purely data-driven projectors.
• Low-rank structure persists: effective stable rank of gradients ≤40 throughout training, validating approach.
Conclusion: Phi-GaLore closes the gap between memory-efficient gradient projection and the stringent symmetry requirements of SciML, enabling billion-parameter PDE solvers and molecular transformers to train on commodity hardware with full-parameter updates. By combining fast randomised sketches, physics-aware bases and cross-layer projector sharing, it removes GaLore’s main bottleneck while improving accuracy in physics-sensitive regimes.
Practically, this unlocks agile experimentation for researchers without multi-GPU clusters, accelerating progress in climate, CFD and drug discovery. Academically, it provides the first systematic study of gradient low-rankness in SciML, introduces symmetry-informed compression and suggests a unifying view that blends GaLore and FLORA. Future work can extend the framework to multi-physics coupling and adaptive rank selection, and explore theoretical bounds on error induced by symmetry-constrained projections.

Experimental Plan 1: Gradient Low-Rankness and Projection Efficiency (micro-bench across SciML backbones)
Goal
• Validate that SciML gradients are low-rank enough for Phi-GaLore and that randomized sketches + tiny SVD achieve high alignment with full gradients while cutting projection overhead.

Models (tiny-to-mid scale, single GPU feasible)
• FNO-Darcy-2D-Tiny (~20M params) on synthetic Darcy flow.
• PINNsFormer-Base (~60M) on 2D Burgers or Navier–Stokes laminar regime (Re ~ 100).
• GeoMFormer-Small (~40M) on a subset of MolPuzzle or QM9 (HOMO-LUMO) to keep runs <12 hours on 1×RTX 4090.

Baselines
• Full-rank AdamW.
• GaLore (rank 64, T=200).
• Phi-GaLore (r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T ∈ {200, 400}).
• Optional: FLORA with 8-bit Adam to test optimizer-state compatibility (use per-layer choose-min-cost switch disabled for this micro-bench).

Measurements
• Gradient low-rankness: stable rank srank = ||G||_F^2 / ||G||_2^2 per large matrix and averaged across steps; top-k energy capture; eigenvalue tail decay.
• Alignment: cos_sim(G, P P^T G) and loss decrease using full vs projected update on a copy of weights (single-step surrogate test).
• Overhead and throughput: time spent in projection, total step time, tokens/s or grid-points/s.
• Memory: peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory estimate.
• Effect of EMA on sketch: alignment vs. noise scale (with/without EMA, α ∈ {0.7, 0.9, 0.98}).
• Hierarchical sharing (enable/disable on attention layers grouped by resolution or depth buckets).

Protocol
1) Train each model for 20k steps with each method; log gradient stats every 100 steps on a fixed batch.
2) For 100 random steps, capture a few largest weight matrices’ dense gradients, compute exact top-128 SVD once (off critical path) to estimate stable rank and energy capture.
3) Compare projection cost between GaLore (full matrix SVD periodically) and Phi-GaLore (CountSketch each step + r×r SVD every T) while keeping r matched.
4) Ablate r and T; ablate EMA factor; ablate hierarchical sharing on transformer blocks.

Success criteria
• Effective stable rank ≤ 40 for most steps and layers.
• Phi-GaLore cos_sim ≥ 0.95 with full-gradient update for r ≥ 32.
• Projection overhead < 5% (vs 14–20% for GaLore at same r); overall throughput ≥ GaLore.

Key Python pieces (PyTorch pseudocode)

# CountSketch for fast subspace sketch (row and column)
class CountSketch:
    def __init__(self, d, r, seed=0):
        g = torch.Generator(device='cuda').manual_seed(seed)
        self.idx = torch.randint(0, r, (d,), generator=g, device='cuda')
        self.sign = torch.where(torch.rand(d, generator=g, device='cuda') > 0.5,
                                torch.tensor(1.0, device='cuda'), torch.tensor(-1.0, device='cuda'))
        self.r = r
    def left(self, X):  # X: [m, n]
        # P_r^T X: sketch rows
        m = X.size(0)
        S = torch.zeros(self.r, X.size(1), device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(0, self.idx[:m], X * self.sign[:m].unsqueeze(1))
        return S
    def right(self, X):  # X: [m, n]
        n = X.size(1)
        S = torch.zeros(X.size(0), self.r, device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(1, self.idx[:n], X * self.sign[:n].unsqueeze(0))
        return S

# per-layer Phi-GaLore state
class PhiGaLoreState:
    def __init__(self, m, n, r=32, ema=0.9, share_key=None):
        self.cs_l = CountSketch(m, r)
        self.cs_r = CountSketch(n, r)
        self.r = r
        self.ema = ema
        self.sketch_ema = torch.zeros(r, r, device='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        self.U = torch.empty(0)  # refined left basis
        self.share_key = share_key
        self.step = 0

    @torch.no_grad()
    def project_grad(self, W, G, B=None, T=400):
        # Stage-1: randomized sketch each step
        S = self.cs_l.left(G)  # [r, n]
        Gt = self.cs_r.right(S)  # [r, r]
        self.sketch_ema = self.ema * self.sketch_ema + (1 - self.ema) * Gt.to(torch.bfloat16)
        self.step += 1
        # Stage-2 every T: tiny SVD on r x r covariance and refine
        if self.step % T == 0:
            C = (self.sketch_ema.float() @ self.sketch_ema.float().T)  # [r, r]
            Uc, _, _ = torch.linalg.svd(C)  # r x r
            Uc = Uc[:, :self.r]
            if B is not None and B.numel() > 0:
                # Orthonormalize [Uc, B] with two Gram–Schmidt passes
                P = torch.cat([Uc, B], dim=1)  # [m_like?, k]
                # Map Uc from sketch row-space back to parameter row-space using left sketch adjoint
                # Approximate lifting by solving min_X ||P_r^T X - Uc||
                # For implementation simplicity in micro-bench, use data-driven U only (set B=None)
                self.U = Uc  # store compact basis proxy in sketch space
            else:
                self.U = Uc
        # Project gradient using current U via two-pass sketching (proxy projection)
        # In micro-bench we evaluate alignment using sketch-space projection quality
        return G  # for actual optimizer, use lifted projector; see Exp 2/3.

# stable rank utility
@torch.no_grad()
def stable_rank(G):
    fro2 = torch.sum(G.float()**2)
    top1 = torch.linalg.norm(G.float(), 2)
    return (fro2 / (top1**2)).item()


Experimental Plan 2: Physics-Aware Subspace Improves PDE Fidelity (Navier–Stokes)
Goal
• Demonstrate that adding analytic symmetry bases B (divergence-free) to the projector reduces physics error and improves stability and generalization to refined meshes and noisy BCs.

Model and data
• PINNsFormer-Large (≈1B) on 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes transient; sequence length 1024. If 1B is infeasible, use PINNsFormer-Base (~200M) with gradient checkpointing.
• Set Reynolds numbers in [100, 1000]; generate training collocation points + boundary data with a CPU CFD solver (or use Airfoil2D benchmarks with synthetic time series).

Symmetry basis B construction
• Goal: favor gradient directions that preserve ∇·u ≈ 0. Use a streamfunction basis ψ_k on the spatial grid so that u = (∂ψ/∂y, −∂ψ/∂x) is divergence-free. Precompute K lowest-frequency Fourier modes or Chebyshev modes; form B_u as the matrix mapping coefficient vector c to velocity field coefficients.
• Map B_u to parameter row-space for output layers that write velocity channels. For a fully-connected last layer W_out ∈ R^{m×n} where m indexes velocity components at collocation points, define B_out ∈ R^{m×k} from the discretized u-basis; for earlier layers, restrict B injection to the last projection into physical space to avoid mismatched semantics.
• Orthonormalize [U_r, B_out] by two-pass Gram–Schmidt; store in bf16.

Baselines and variants
• Full-rank AdamW.
• GaLore (r=64).
• Phi-GaLore without B (data-driven only).
• Phi-GaLore with B, K ∈ {8, 16, 32}.
• Ablations: r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T ∈ {200, 400}, with/without hierarchical sharing across attention value matrices.

Metrics
• Relative L2 error on velocity/pressure vs. reference solver on held-out IC/BCs.
• Volume-averaged PDE residuals: ||∂tu + u·∇u + ∇p − νΔu||_2 and ||∇·u||_2.
• Stability under 2× mesh refinement: rollout 200 steps; measure divergence drift and kinetic energy spectrum error.
• Compute and log stable rank of gradients and projector overhead.

Protocol
1) Train each method for 150k steps (or budget-limited steps) on 2×RTX 4090 using DDP, mixed precision, gradient checkpointing for 1B model.
2) Inject B only for last two layers that map to physical fields; update B every T with fixed K.
3) Evaluate on clean test BCs and robustness stressors: add 1% and 5% Gaussian noise to BCs; random jitter of mesh nodes (1% domain size).
4) Record wall-clock time to reach rL2 ≤ target (e.g., 1e-2), divergence norm, and projection overhead.

Success criteria
• With B: ≥ 8% lower rL2 versus Phi-GaLore without B at matched r; lower divergence norm and better spectral match.
• Projection overhead still < 5% and throughput ≥ GaLore; accuracy within 1% of Full-rank.

Key Python pieces (projector with B on output layers)

# Build divergence-free basis on Nx x Ny grid using low-frequency Fourier modes
def build_divfree_basis(Nx, Ny, K):
    xs = torch.linspace(0, 2*torch.pi, steps=Nx, device='cuda')
    ys = torch.linspace(0, 2*torch.pi, steps=Ny, device='cuda')
    X, Y = torch.meshgrid(xs, ys, indexing='ij')
    modes = []
    for kx in range(1, int(K**0.5)+1):
        for ky in range(1, int(K**0.5)+1):
            psi = torch.sin(kx*X) * torch.sin(ky*Y)
            ux = torch.autograd.grad(psi.sum(), Y, retain_graph=True, create_graph=False)[0] if False else kx*torch.cos(kx*X)*torch.sin(ky*Y)  # analytical derivative
            uy = -(ky*torch.sin(kx*X)*torch.cos(ky*Y))
            modes.append(torch.stack([ux, uy], dim=0))  # [2, Nx, Ny]
            if len(modes) >= K: break
        if len(modes) >= K: break
    B = torch.stack(modes, dim=-1)  # [2, Nx, Ny, K]
    B = B.reshape(2*Nx*Ny, K)  # match m for velocity outputs
    # Orthonormalize
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(B.float(), mode='reduced')
    return Q[:, :K].to(torch.bfloat16)

# Apply in optimizer wrapper for the last layer mapping to velocity
# Given gradient G_out [m, n] and basis B_out [m, K]
@torch.no_grad()
def project_with_basis(G_out, U_r, B_out):
    # Combine data-driven U_r (lifted to row-space) and analytic B_out
    # For simplicity: orthonormalize B_out and compute projection using B only when U_r unavailable
    P = B_out.float()  # [m, k]
    return P @ (P.T @ G_out.float())


Experimental Plan 3: Memory-Constrained Billion-Parameter Training with Hierarchical Sharing (molecular transformer)
Goal
• Show that Phi-GaLore enables 1–1.3B parameter SciML transformers to train within 24 GB per GPU with improved throughput and accuracy competitive to Full-rank and better than GaLore/LoRA; verify cross-task generality on molecular data and evaluate rotational symmetry bases.

Model and data
• GeoMFormer-Base (~1B) or 1.3B variant for HOMO-LUMO prediction on MolPuzzle; fallback: 300–500M replication on QM9+ extension for smaller labs.
• Inputs: 3D coordinates and atomic types; use e3nn for SO(3)-equivariant components.

Symmetry basis B
• Rotation-aware basis using low-order spherical harmonics Y_lm (l ≤ 2) to encode SO(3) structure. For attention value matrices that map geometric features, build B from block-diagonal expansions aligned with irreps (l=0,1,2) so that projected gradients preserve equivariant mixing constraints. Precompute block bases per irrep and share them across layers at the same resolution (hierarchical sharing factor ≥ 8×).

Setup
• Hardware: 2×RTX 4090 (24 GB) with FSDP zero2 or DDP + activation checkpointing; bf16 compute; 8-bit Adam for states.
• Optimizer: Phi-GaLore wrapper around AdamW; enable per-layer choose-min-cost with FLORA if its momentum compression is cheaper; keep EMA sketch and B in bf16.

Comparisons
• Full-rank AdamW (on A100-80GB for reference if 4090 OOM; report accuracy/throughput).
• LoRA rank-64 fine-tuning (init from pretrained if available; otherwise train-from-scratch baseline at smaller scale).
• GaLore rank-64, T=200.
• Phi-GaLore r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T=400, sharing across attention V and output projections by depth bucket.

Metrics
• MAE on HOMO-LUMO; Spearman-ρ; robustness to conformer noise (random rotations/perturbations of 3D structures).
• Peak memory and optimizer-state memory; projection overhead; tokens/s or graphs/s; wall-clock to reach a fixed MAE.
• Gradient stable rank for representative layers; ablation of sharing factor and symmetry basis.

Protocol
1) Configure FSDP/ZeRO with parameter sharding and activation checkpointing; verify memory headroom at init.
2) Train for 150k steps; batch size tuned to fill memory headroom for each method.
3) Enable hierarchical sharing: group layers by stage (early, mid, late) and reuse projectors within a group; recompute tiny SVD on group EMA sketch every T.
4) Evaluate test MAE and ρ; run robustness test with random rotations and 0.05 Å Gaussian coordinate noise.
5) Log memory (torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated), optimizer-state footprint (sum over params of states’ dtypes), and per-step time; compute projection overhead.

Success criteria
• Fits 1.0–1.3B model on 2×4090 with Phi-GaLore but not with Full-rank; optimizer-state memory reduced by 60–68% vs Full-rank and 10–15% vs GaLore.
• Projection overhead < 5%; throughput +18% vs GaLore; accuracy within 1% of Full-rank and ≥ LoRA.
• With SO(3) basis, modest accuracy gain vs Phi-GaLore without B and improved robustness to rotations.

Core optimizer wrapper sketch (applicable to Exp 2 and 3)

class PhiGaLore(torch.optim.Optimizer):
    def __init__(self, params, base_opt, r=32, T=400, ema=0.9, share_by=None, symmetry_registry=None):
        self.base_opt = base_opt
        self.r = r; self.T = T; self.ema = ema
        self.symmetry_registry = symmetry_registry or {}
        self.layer_states = {}
        self.share_groups = {}
        # share_by: callable(param) -> share_key for hierarchical sharing

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self, closure=None):
        loss = None
        if closure is not None:
            loss = closure()
        # 1) build/update sketches per share_key
        for p in self.base_opt.param_groups[0]['params']:
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:  # only matrix-like here; others default
                continue
            m, n = p.grad.shape
            key = share_by(p) if share_by else id(p)
            st = self.layer_states.get(key)
            if st is None:
                st = PhiGaLoreState(m, n, r=self.r, ema=self.ema, share_key=key)
                self.layer_states[key] = st
            S = st.cs_l.left(p.grad)  # [r, n]
            Gt = st.cs_r.right(S)     # [r, r]
            st.sketch_ema = self.ema * st.sketch_ema + (1 - self.ema) * Gt.to(torch.bfloat16)
            st.step += 1
        # 2) periodic tiny SVD + refinement per group
        for key, st in self.layer_states.items():
            if st.step % self.T == 0:
                C = st.sketch_ema.float() @ st.sketch_ema.float().T
                Uc, _, _ = torch.linalg.svd(C)
                st.U = Uc[:, :self.r].contiguous()  # stored in sketch space
        # 3) apply projection to each param grad using current projector; if symmetry basis exists, combine
        for p in self.base_opt.param_groups[0]['params']:
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            key = share_by(p) if share_by else id(p)
            st = self.layer_states[key]
            B = self.symmetry_registry.get(key)  # optional B mapped to row-space of p
            if B is not None:
                # Project using B; in practice combine lifted U and B. Here we show B-only for clarity on critical layers.
                P = B.float()
                p.grad.data = (P @ (P.T @ p.grad.float())).to(p.grad.dtype)
            else:
                # Fallback: use unprojected grad when lifted U is not available; practical impl would lift st.U via sketch adjoint.
                pass
        # 4) call base optimizer
        self.base_opt.step()
        return loss


General notes and practical tips
• Start with tiny models to validate correctness and profiling, then scale.
• Use torch.compile where available and set matmul precision to high for bf16 stability.
• Log stable rank and alignment on a small subset of layers to avoid overhead.
• For symmetry bases, restrict B to output layers mapping to physical or equivariant quantities to ensure semantic consistency.
• For hierarchical sharing, group by depth or resolution; recompute group projector every T and cache per group.

Collective validation across the three experiments
• Exp 1 establishes that gradients in SciML are low-rank and that CountSketch + tiny SVD suffices.
• Exp 2 shows physics-aware refinement matters, improving PDE fidelity and robustness.
• Exp 3 demonstrates scalability and memory/throughput gains on billion-parameter SciML transformers with cross-task generality and projector sharing.
experimental_design.experiment_details:
This specification expands each experiment in the Experiment Strategy into implementable, reliable PyTorch studies with concrete procedures, instrumentation, and code sketches. It assumes BF16 mixed precision training, distributed data parallel or FSDP where needed, and strong emphasis on accurate profiling and fair baselines.

Global setup and reproducibility
- Hardware: 1×RTX 4090 24 GB for micro-bench; 2×RTX 4090 24 GB or 1×A100-80GB for large runs.
- Software: PyTorch ≥ 2.3, CUDA ≥ 12.x, xFormers ≥ 0.0.26, bitsandbytes ≥ 0.43, e3nn ≥ 0.5, torch_geometric ≥ 2.5 (optional for molecular), neuraloperator ≥ 0.2 (for FNO and Darcy). Optional: wandb for logging.
- Dtypes: bfloat16 compute (torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')), parameters in fp32 unless using FSDP mixed-precision; optimizer states in 8-bit (where applicable) via bitsandbytes.
- Seeds: torch.manual_seed(42), numpy.random.seed(42), Python hash seed set; 3 seeds for each key result, report mean ± 95% CI (bootstrap with 1k resamples for accuracy metrics and Spearman-ρ).
- Logging and profiling: pytorch-lightning or vanilla PyTorch with wandb. Use torch.profiler for selective steps (avoid constant overhead). Use CUDA events to time projection vs. total step.
- Gradient capture safety: only materialize dense gradients for a few largest matrices and at low frequency off the critical path; synchronize CUDA events before timing readouts.

Core: Phi-GaLore primitives and optimizer wrapper
- Randomized sketching: CountSketch left (rows) and right (cols). Maintain EMA of r×r core sketch to suppress stochastic noise.
- Tiny SVD: every T steps, SVD of r×r covariance; combine with physics symmetry bases B where applicable; orthonormalize with QR.
- Lifting from sketch space to row-space: approximate inverse sketch to construct a row-space basis P_m×k from U_r using counts normalization; re-orthonormalize with QR for numerical stability.
- Hierarchical sharing: group parameters by a share_key (e.g., attention V/out projection at same resolution or depth bucket). Share sketches, EMA, and tiny SVD per group.
- Optimizer integration: a wrapper around AdamW (or bitsandbytes Adam8bit) that projects per-parameter gradients before base optimizer step. Switch off projection for vectors and small matrices below a size threshold.

Code: Phi-GaLore utilities (PyTorch, minimal custom logic)

class CountSketch:
    def __init__(self, d, r, device='cuda', seed=0):
        g = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
        self.idx = torch.randint(low=0, high=r, size=(d,), generator=g, device=device)
        self.sign = torch.where(torch.rand(d, generator=g, device=device) > 0.5,
                                torch.tensor(1.0, device=device), torch.tensor(-1.0, device=device))
        self.r = r
        self.d = d
        self.device = device

    @torch.no_grad()
    def left(self, X):  # X: [m, n], returns [r, n]
        S = torch.zeros(self.r, X.size(1), device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(0, self.idx[:X.size(0)], X * self.sign[:X.size(0)].unsqueeze(1))
        return S

    @torch.no_grad()
    def right(self, X):  # X: [m, n], returns [m, r]
        S = torch.zeros(X.size(0), self.r, device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(1, self.idx[:X.size(1)], X * self.sign[:X.size(1)].unsqueeze(0))
        return S

@torch.no_grad()
def unsketch_rows(U_sketch, cs_left):
    # Lift from sketch space [r, k] to row-space [m, k] using unsketch via bucket expansion and count normalization
    m = cs_left.d
    r = cs_left.r
    counts = torch.bincount(cs_left.idx[:m], minlength=r).clamp_min(1).to(U_sketch.device)
    inv_sqrt = (1.0 / counts.float()).sqrt().unsqueeze(1)  # [r,1]
    U_scaled = U_sketch.float() * inv_sqrt  # [r,k]
    P = torch.zeros(m, U_sketch.size(1), device=U_sketch.device, dtype=U_sketch.dtype)
    P.index_add_(0, cs_left.idx[:m], U_scaled * cs_left.sign[:m].unsqueeze(1))
    # Orthonormalize to improve numerical stability
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(P.float(), mode='reduced')
    return Q.contiguous()

@torch.no_grad()
def project_grad_with_basis(G, P=None, B=None):
    # G: [m, n]; P: [m, kp] learned basis; B: [m, kb] physics basis; returns projected gradient
    components = []
    if P is not None and P.numel() > 0:
        components.append(P.float())
    if B is not None and B.numel() > 0:
        # Orthonormalize and remove redundancy when concatenated
        if len(components) > 0:
            Pcat = torch.cat([components[0].float(), B.float()], dim=1)
        else:
            Pcat = B.float()
        Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(Pcat, mode='reduced')
        Puse = Q
    else:
        Puse = components[0] if len(components) > 0 else None
    if Puse is None:
        return G  # no projection
    return (Puse @ (Puse.T @ G.float())).to(G.dtype)

class PhiGaLoreGroupState:
    def __init__(self, m, n, r, ema, device='cuda', seed=0):
        self.cs_l = CountSketch(m, r, device=device, seed=seed)
        self.cs_r = CountSketch(n, r, device=device, seed=seed+1)
        self.r = r
        self.ema = ema
        self.sketch_ema = torch.zeros(r, r, device=device, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        self.step = 0
        self.U_sketch = None  # [r, k]
        self.U_row = None     # [m, k]

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update_sketch(self, G):
        S = self.cs_l.left(G)    # [r, n]
        Gt = self.cs_r.right(S)  # [r, r]
        self.sketch_ema = self.ema * self.sketch_ema + (1.0 - self.ema) * Gt.to(torch.bfloat16)
        self.step += 1

    @torch.no_grad()
    def refine_basis(self, k=None):
        # r x r tiny SVD
        C = self.sketch_ema.float() @ self.sketch_ema.float().T
        Uc, Svals, _ = torch.linalg.svd(C)
        k_use = k if k is not None else self.r
        self.U_sketch = Uc[:, :k_use].contiguous()  # [r, k]
        self.U_row = None  # force re-lift when needed

    @torch.no_grad()
    def lift_if_needed(self):
        if self.U_row is None and self.U_sketch is not None:
            self.U_row = unsketch_rows(self.U_sketch, self.cs_l)  # [m, k]
        return self.U_row

class PhiGaLoreWrapper:
    def __init__(self, model, base_opt, r=32, T=400, ema=0.9, share_by=None, symmetry_registry=None,
                 large_only_threshold=16384):
        self.model = model
        self.base_opt = base_opt
        self.r = r
        self.T = T
        self.ema = ema
        self.share_by = share_by
        self.symmetry_registry = symmetry_registry or {}
        self.group_states = {}
        self.large_only_threshold = large_only_threshold
        self.last_step = 0
        self._ev_proj_start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        self._ev_proj_end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        self._proj_ms = 0.0

    def group_key(self, name, param):
        return self.share_by(name, param) if self.share_by is not None else name

    @torch.no_grad()
    def pre_step_projection(self):
        self._ev_proj_start.record()
        # 1) update sketches per group using first occurrence of gradient per group
        seen = set()
        for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            if p.numel() < self.large_only_threshold:
                continue
            key = self.group_key(name, p)
            if key not in seen:
                seen.add(key)
                m, n = p.grad.shape
                st = self.group_states.get(key)
                if st is None:
                    st = PhiGaLoreGroupState(m, n, r=self.r, ema=self.ema, device=p.grad.device)
                    self.group_states[key] = st
                st.update_sketch(p.grad)
        # 2) periodic tiny SVD per group
        for key, st in self.group_states.items():
            if st.step > 0 and st.step % self.T == 0:
                st.refine_basis(k=self.r)
        # 3) project each grad with combined learned and physics bases
        for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            if p.numel() < self.large_only_threshold:
                continue
            key = self.group_key(name, p)
            st = self.group_states[key]
            U_row = st.lift_if_needed()
            B = self.symmetry_registry.get(key)  # optional physics basis [m, kb]
            p.grad.data = project_grad_with_basis(p.grad.data, P=U_row, B=B)
        self._ev_proj_end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        self._proj_ms = self._ev_proj_start.elapsed_time(self._ev_proj_end)

    def step(self):
        self.pre_step_projection()
        self.base_opt.step()

    def zero_grad(self, set_to_none=True):
        self.base_opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=set_to_none)

    def projection_overhead_ms(self):
        return self._proj_ms

Utilities: gradient diagnostics and alignment tests

@torch.no_grad()
def stable_rank(G):
    Gf = G.float()
    fro2 = torch.sum(Gf * Gf)
    top1 = torch.linalg.norm(Gf, 2)
    return (fro2 / (top1 * top1)).item()

@torch.no_grad()
def topk_energy(G, k):
    # For sampled large matrices only; heavy, run sparsely
    U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(G.float(), full_matrices=False)
    energy = (S * S)
    total = energy.sum().item()
    top = energy[:k].sum().item()
    return top / (total + 1e-12)

@torch.no_grad()
def cos_sim_full_vs_projected(model, loss_fn, batch, optimizer_wrapper, target_param_names):
    # Single-step surrogate alignment on a copy of weights
    # 1) compute full gradient
    loss = loss_fn(model(**batch))
    loss.backward()
    grads_full = {n: p.grad.detach().clone() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if n in target_param_names}
    # 2) projected gradient using wrapper (without stepping base opt)
    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss2 = loss_fn(model(**batch))
    loss2.backward()
    optimizer_wrapper.pre_step_projection()
    grads_proj = {n: p.grad.detach().clone() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if n in target_param_names}
    # 3) cosine similarity
    cos_sims = {}
    for n in target_param_names:
        g = grads_full[n].flatten().float()
        gp = grads_proj[n].flatten().float()
        cos = torch.dot(g, gp) / (g.norm() * gp.norm() + 1e-12)
        cos_sims[n] = cos.item()
    model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    return cos_sims


Experimental Plan 1: Gradient Low-Rankness and Projection Efficiency (micro-bench)
Goal
- Validate low-rankness of SciML gradients.
- Show Phi-GaLore alignment to full gradients with low overhead and memory.

Models
- FNO-Darcy-2D-Tiny (~20M): import from neuraloperator; dataset DarcyFlow (prepackaged) 64×64 grids. Batch size 8–16 on 4090.
- PINNsFormer-Base (~60M): a compact transformer-like PINN for 2D Burgers or laminar Navier–Stokes (Re≈100). If unavailable, use a U-Net or small transformer head predicting u, v, p on 128×128 grid with physics-informed loss (residual collocation + boundary losses). Batch size 4–8.
- GeoMFormer-Small (~40M): equivariant transformer using e3nn for HOMO-LUMO on QM9 subset or MolPuzzle subset. Batch size 32 graphs.

Baselines
- Full-rank AdamW (fp32 params, bf16 compute).
- GaLore (rank=64, T=200) from a public implementation if available; otherwise replicate: full SVD of target matrices every T and project gradients. Use torch.linalg.svd on each parameter matrix targeted by GaLore.
- Phi-GaLore (r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T ∈ {200, 400}), EMA α ∈ {0.7, 0.9, 0.98}.
- Optional: FLORA + 8-bit Adam (bitsandbytes Adam8bit) as a separate run for compatibility check; do not enable per-layer switch in this micro-bench.

Measurements and instrumentation
- Gradient low-rankness: per step (every 100 steps) for 2–3 largest matrices per model, log stable rank srank = ||G||_F^2 / ||G||_2^2, top-k energy capture (k ∈ {16, 32, 64, 128}). Compute exact SVD on those sampled steps only (100 random steps across 20k).
- Alignment: cosine similarity between full gradient and Phi-GaLore projected gradient for the same step on selected matrices (cos_sim ≥ 0.95 target at r ≥ 32).
- Overhead and throughput: measure projection time via CUDA events inside wrapper; log iteration time and samples/s (or grid-points/s) via wall-clock (time.perf_counter) excluding validation.
- Memory: torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated and optimizer-state size estimate: sum over params of states multiplied by dtype size (for AdamW, 2 state tensors per param; for 8-bit Adam, assume 2 bytes per element for quantized states plus optimizer-specific overhead from bitsandbytes). Record peak VRAM using torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved.
- Effect of EMA: run identical configs varying α; log cos_sim and srank scatterplots.
- Hierarchical sharing: for transformer models, group by block depth (e.g., blocks 0–3 share, 4–7 share). Toggle sharing on/off and compare overhead and alignment.

Protocol
1) Train each model for 20k steps for each method, same batch size, learning rate schedule (cosine decay or constant), warmup 1k steps, weight decay 0.01 (AdamW). Enable grad clipping at 1.0.
2) Every 100 steps, on a fixed held batch (clone inputs to avoid nondeterministic augmentation), compute gradient snapshots and record srank, top-k energy for selected parameters.
3) For 100 randomly chosen steps per run, compute exact top-128 SVD of those gradients; do not block the training loop: use a background CUDA stream or perform during validation to amortize overhead.
4) Profile 50 representative steps per method with torch.profiler to attribute time to projection vs. matmul and attention.
5) Ablations: r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T ∈ {200, 400}, EMA α ∈ {0.7, 0.9, 0.98}, sharing on/off (for transformer only). Each ablation at least 3 seeds.

Key training snippet: wrapping optimizer

model = build_model()
base_opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.01)
# Optional 8-bit Adam
# base_opt = bitsandbytes.optim.AdamW8bit(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.01)

def share_by(name, p):
    # Example grouping: attention V and out projection by depth bucket extracted from module name
    # expects names like 'blocks.03.attn.v.weight'
    parts = name.split('.')
    key = None
    if 'attn' in parts and ('v' in parts or 'out_proj' in parts):
        # bucket depths in groups of 4
        for i, tok in enumerate(parts):
            if tok.isdigit():
                depth = int(tok)
                bucket = depth // 4
                key = f'group.attn.bucket{bucket}'
                break
    return key or name

phi = PhiGaLoreWrapper(model, base_opt, r=32, T=400, ema=0.9, share_by=share_by)

for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    base_opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    with torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        out = model(**batch)
        loss = loss_fn(out, batch['y'])
    loss.backward()
    phi.step()
    if step % 100 == 0:
        print(f'step {step} proj_overhead_ms {phi.projection_overhead_ms():.3f}')

Success criteria
- Effective stable rank ≤ 40 across most steps and layers.
- Phi-GaLore cosine similarity ≥ 0.95 with full gradient at r ≥ 32; ≥ 0.9 at r=16.
- Projection overhead < 5% of step time; throughput ≥ GaLore; tokens/s or grid-points/s improves over GaLore by ≥ 15%.
- Memory: optimizer-state memory reduction consistent with 60–68% vs. full-rank; 10–15% vs. GaLore with sharing enabled.

Reliability enhancements
- Repeat 3 seeds per ablation; report mean ± 95% CI.
- Verify reproducibility by checkpointing RNG states and re-running 100 steps to match logs within tolerance.
- Sanity-check: disable projection (identity) and ensure metrics match Full-rank baseline.


Experimental Plan 2: Physics-Aware Subspace Improves PDE Fidelity (Navier–Stokes)
Goal
- Demonstrate that adding analytic divergence-free bases B reduces rL2 error, divergence norm, and improves stability on refined meshes and noisy BCs.

Model and data
- Preferred: PINNsFormer-Large (~1B) for 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes transient on 1024 pseudo-sequence length. If infeasible on 2×4090, use PINNsFormer-Base (~200–300M) with activation checkpointing and FSDP sharding.
- Data generation: For 2D cavity or airfoil flow, generate collocation points (interior + boundary) using Halton or Sobol sequences; use a CPU CFD reference for supervision on a subset (or self-supervised PINN residuals). Alternatively, use Modulus or simple finite-difference solver on 256×256 grid to produce targets for supervised residual.
- Reynolds in [100, 1000], viscosity ν configured accordingly.

Physics basis B construction
- Build divergence-free velocity basis on Nx×Ny grid via low-frequency Fourier streamfunction modes ψ_k(x, y) such that u = (∂ψ/∂y, −∂ψ/∂x). Select K ∈ {8, 16, 32} low frequencies; stack into B_out ∈ R^{(2·Nx·Ny)×K}. Orthonormalize with QR, store bf16.
- Attach B_out only to final projection layers mapping hidden features to velocity channels (and optionally pressure). Do not force B on early layers to avoid semantic mismatch.
- Update B_out if grid changes; otherwise keep fixed across training. For mesh refinement evaluation, interpolate B to refined grid using spectral interpolation (FFT zero-padding) or bilinear upsampling.

Code: building divergence-free basis on grid

def build_divfree_basis_fourier(Nx, Ny, K, device='cuda'):
    xs = torch.linspace(0, 2*torch.pi, steps=Nx, device=device)
    ys = torch.linspace(0, 2*torch.pi, steps=Ny, device=device)
    X, Y = torch.meshgrid(xs, ys, indexing='ij')
    modes = []
    max_k = int(max(1, K ** 0.5)) + 1
    for kx in range(1, max_k):
        for ky in range(1, max_k):
            if len(modes) >= K: break
            psi = torch.sin(kx * X) * torch.sin(ky * Y)
            ux = kx * torch.cos(kx * X) * torch.sin(ky * Y)   # ∂ψ/∂y up to scaling; we use orthonormalization later
            uy = -(ky * torch.sin(kx * X) * torch.cos(ky * Y))
            modes.append(torch.stack([ux, uy], dim=0))  # [2, Nx, Ny]
        if len(modes) >= K: break
    B = torch.stack(modes, dim=-1)  # [2, Nx, Ny, K]
    B = B.reshape(2*Nx*Ny, K)
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(B.float(), mode='reduced')
    return Q[:, :K].to(torch.bfloat16)

Wiring B into Phi-GaLore (last layers only)
- Identify output layers by module names (e.g., 'head_vel.weight'). Compute m from that parameter shape and reshape B to match row dimension ordering.
- Register B in wrapper.symmetry_registry with the group key corresponding to that layer (or its share group if shared).

symmetry_registry = {}
# suppose model.head_vel.weight has shape [2*Nx*Ny, hidden]
B_out = build_divfree_basis_fourier(Nx, Ny, K=16)
symmetry_registry['head_vel.weight'] = B_out
phi = PhiGaLoreWrapper(model, base_opt, r=32, T=400, ema=0.9, share_by=share_by, symmetry_registry=symmetry_registry)

PDE residual metrics
- rL2 on velocity/pressure: ||pred − ref||_2 / ||ref||_2 across domain and time.
- Divergence norm: mean ||∇·u||_2 over domain.
- PDE residual norm: mean ||∂t u + u·∇u + ∇p − νΔu||_2 computed via finite differences (5-point stencil) implemented by conv2d on channel-stacked fields.
- Stability under 2× mesh refinement: bilinearly interpolate model outputs or re-evaluate model on denser grid; rollout 200 steps with explicit scheme and measure drift in divergence and kinetic energy spectrum error E(k) vs. reference.

Code: divergence and Laplacian by convolution (periodic or reflective BCs configurable)

def spatial_derivatives(u, padding='replicate'):
    # u: [B, 2, Nx, Ny]; returns div, laplacian
    kx = torch.tensor([[0, 0, 0], [-0.5, 0, 0.5], [0, 0, 0]], device=u.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3)
    ky = torch.tensor([[0, -0.5, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0.5, 0]], device=u.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3)
    lap = torch.tensor([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]], device=u.device).view(1, 1, 3, 3)
    ux = torch.nn.functional.conv2d(u[:, 0:1], kx, padding=1)
    uy = torch.nn.functional.conv2d(u[:, 1:2], ky, padding=1)
    div = ux + uy
    uxx = torch.nn.functional.conv2d(u[:, 0:1], lap, padding=1)
    uyy = torch.nn.functional.conv2d(u[:, 1:2], lap, padding=1)
    return div, torch.cat([uxx, uyy], dim=1)

Training and evaluation protocol
1) Configure DDP over 2×4090 (or A100-80GB single). Enable activation checkpointing on transformer blocks; BF16 autocast.
2) Train for 150k steps for each of: Full-rank, GaLore (r=64), Phi-GaLore without B, Phi-GaLore with B (K∈{8, 16, 32}); ablate r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T ∈ {200, 400}. Keep all other hyperparams fixed.
3) Robustness tests: add Gaussian noise N(0, σ) to boundary conditions with σ ∈ {0.01, 0.05}×scale; jitter mesh nodes by 1% of domain size and recompute PDE residuals; evaluate rL2 and divergence norms.
4) Stability tests: run 200-step rollout on 2× refined mesh; compute kinetic energy spectrum via FFT of velocity field; measure L2 error over wavenumbers.
5) Record projection overhead %, throughput, and wall-clock to reach rL2 ≤ 1e-2.

Success criteria
- With B: ≥ 8% lower rL2 vs. Phi-GaLore without B at matched r; lower divergence norm and better spectral match.
- Projection overhead < 5%, throughput ≥ GaLore; accuracy within 1% of Full-rank.

Reliability enhancements
- Freeze learning rate schedule and data seeds across methods.
- Measure gradient srank concurrently to link performance gains to low-rankness persistence.
- Early-stop only for wall-clock-to-target metric; otherwise train full 150k steps for fair area-under-curve comparisons.


Experimental Plan 3: Memory-Constrained Billion-Parameter Training with Hierarchical Sharing (molecular transformer)
Goal
- Validate that Phi-GaLore enables 1–1.3B parameter SciML transformers within 24 GB/GPU with <5% overhead, improved throughput vs. GaLore, and accuracy within 1% of Full-rank.
- Demonstrate SO(3)-aware symmetry bases B improve robustness to rotations and small conformer noise.

Model and data
- GeoMFormer-Base/XL (~1.0–1.3B) for HOMO-LUMO regression. If needed, run a 300–500M variant for feasibility and scale conclusions by extrapolation.
- Build on an equivariant backbone using e3nn. Use PyTorch Geometric to load QM9 for fallback; for MolPuzzle (217 molecules), load structures with RDKit and generate multiple conformers per molecule.
- Data augmentations: random rotations, Gaussian coordinate noise 0.05 Å; ensure label invariance.

SO(3) symmetry basis B
- For attention value/output projection matrices that mix features of irreps l=0,1,2, constrain projected gradients to preserve equivariant mixing by injecting block bases aligned with irreps.
- Construct B per layer group: for a parameter with row-dimension m corresponding to concatenated irreps across nodes, build a block-diagonal basis P_block where each block is an identity in the space of an irrep channel and zeros elsewhere. Augment with low-order spherical harmonics Y_lm evaluated at canonical orientations to encode rotation structure; orthonormalize and share across layers of same resolution.

Code sketch: building equivariant block basis using e3nn

from e3nn.o3 import spherical_harmonics

def build_so3_block_basis(irrep_counts, K_extra=0, device='cuda'):
    # irrep_counts: dict like {'0e': c0, '1e': c1, '2e': c2} giving counts of channels per irrep
    # Build block identity basis that preserves channel mixing within same irrep types
    blocks = []
    offset = 0
    for ir, c in irrep_counts.items():
        if c == 0: continue
        # For each channel in this irrep, allocate basis vector that selects it
        I = torch.eye(c, device=device)
        # Expand to row space segment [offset:offset+c]
        B_ir = I  # [c, c]
        blocks.append((offset, B_ir))
        offset += c
    # Assemble into a big sparse-like block matrix then densify
    m = sum(irrep_counts.values())
    k = sum(c for c in irrep_counts.values())
    B = torch.zeros(m, k, device=device)
    col = 0
    row_offset = 0
    for ir, c in irrep_counts.items():
        if c == 0: continue
        B[row_offset:row_offset+c, col:col+c] = torch.eye(c, device=device)
        col += c
        row_offset += c
    # Optionally augment with low-order Y_lm evaluated on canonical directions (x, y, z) if row semantics map to directions
    if K_extra > 0:
        dirs = torch.tensor([[1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1]], dtype=torch.float32, device=device)
        Y = [spherical_harmonics(l, dirs, normalize=True) for l in [0,1,2]]  # list of [dirs, 2l+1]
        Ycat = torch.cat([y for y in Y], dim=1)  # [3, 1+3+5]
        Ycat = Ycat[:min(3, K_extra), :]
        Ycat = torch.nn.functional.normalize(Ycat, dim=0)
        B = torch.cat([B, torch.randn(m, Ycat.size(1), device=device) * 0.0], dim=1)  # placeholder alignment, keep block identity dominant
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(B.float(), mode='reduced')
    return Q.to(torch.bfloat16)

Note: The exact mapping from parameter rows to irrep channels depends on the model implementation. In practice, we derive irrep_counts from the module's e3nn.Lines or tensor product definitions. We restrict B to parameters that map equivariant features to outputs or between equivariant spaces; other matrices use Phi-GaLore learned basis only.

Training system configuration
- Parallelism: FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) with ZeRO2 stage to shard parameters and optimizer states across 2 GPUs. Use auto_wrap_policy to wrap transformer blocks; CPU offload disabled to avoid PCIe bottlenecks.
- Memory saving: activation checkpointing on attention/MLP blocks; xFormers memory efficient attention; bf16 mixed precision; bitsandbytes Adam8bit.
- Batch size: choose per method to saturate memory without OOM; scale learning rate accordingly (linear scale with global batch).
- Hierarchical sharing: group by model stage (early, mid, late) and matrix type (attention V, out projections, FFN first/second linear). Use a share factor ≥ 8× for attention V and out projections. Update tiny SVD per group every T steps.
- Optional per-layer choose-min-cost between Phi-GaLore and FLORA: if FLORA is available, measure per-group projection/comp overhead during warmup 100 steps and select the cheaper route for that group for the remainder of training.

Protocol
1) Initialize model and FSDP; run a dry pass to estimate memory headroom per method; set batch size accordingly.
2) Train for 150k steps per method: Full-rank (A100-80GB reference if 4090 OOM), LoRA (rank-64) fine-tuning if pretrained exists, GaLore (rank-64, T=200), Phi-GaLore (r ∈ {16, 32, 64}, T=400) with hierarchical sharing; Phi-GaLore+SO(3) symmetry basis on targeted layers.
3) Log MAE on HOMO-LUMO and Spearman-ρ each epoch; robustness: evaluate test set under random rotations (uniform SO(3)) and 0.05 Å Gaussian coordinate noise. Ensure prediction is rotation-invariant; any degradation indicates sensitivity.
4) Log peak memory, optimizer-state memory (sum over params of states size × dtype), projection overhead %, tokens/graphs per second, and wall-clock to reach a fixed MAE threshold.
5) Gradient diagnostics: srank for representative large matrices every 500 steps and top-k energy on 50 sampled steps.

Memory accounting utility

def optimizer_state_bytes(params, adam_bits=32):
    # Adam has 2 states per param; with bitsandbytes 8-bit, treat as 1 byte per state plus scaling overhead (~0.5x); approximate here
    total_elems = sum(p.numel() for p in params)
    if adam_bits == 32:
        return total_elems * 2 * 4  # 2 states, float32
    elif adam_bits == 16:
        return total_elems * 2 * 2
    elif adam_bits == 8:
        return int(total_elems * 2 * 1.5)  # 8-bit + scales/metadata approx
    else:
        return total_elems * 2 * 4

Success criteria
- Fit 1.0–1.3B parameter model on 2×4090 with Phi-GaLore (peak < 24 GB per GPU) while Full-rank fails to fit; optimizer-state memory reduced by 60–68% vs. full-rank and 10–15% vs. GaLore.
- Projection overhead < 5%; throughput +18% vs. GaLore; accuracy within 1% of Full-rank and ≥ LoRA.
- With SO(3) basis B, modest gains over Phi-GaLore without B and improved robustness to rotations and conformer noise.

Reliability and fairness
- Same data splits and augmentations across methods; identical LR schedule, warmup, and weight decay.
- Freeze random seeds for architecture instantiation and data order; 3 seeds per method.
- Report 95% bootstrap CI for MAE and Spearman-ρ; paired t-test between Phi-GaLore with/without B on robustness metrics.


Cross-experiment integration and non-overlap
- Exp 1 establishes low-rankness and validates sketch+tiny SVD alignment, while profiling overheads and sharing at small scale.
- Exp 2 focuses on physics-aware subspaces for PDE fidelity and robustness; only a subset of layers gets B to avoid confounds and to respect semantics.
- Exp 3 scales to billion-parameter, introduces hierarchical projector sharing aggressively and SO(3) bases; emphasizes memory/throughput and cross-task generality.
- Shared components (sketching, tiny SVD, lifting, logging) are reused to ensure comparability; measurement code is unified to reduce duplication.

Risk mitigation and practical tips
- If lifting from sketch yields poor alignment early in training, temporarily increase r to 64 for first 5k steps, then drop to target r.
- Use two-pass QR for P concatenated with B to eliminate near-collinearity; in bf16, temporarily upcast to fp32 for orthonormalization.
- Skip projection for small matrices (< 16k elements) where overhead may outweigh gains.
- Ensure that symmetry bases are only applied to layers with well-defined physical row semantics (e.g., velocity outputs), otherwise use data-driven basis only.
- For GaLore baseline, cap SVD frequency at T=200 and target only large matrices to keep wall-clock feasible; log its projection time to ensure fair comparison.

Expected outcomes summary
- Exp 1: stable rank consistently ≤ 40; Phi-GaLore alignment cos_sim ≥ 0.95 at r ≥ 32; overhead < 5% vs. GaLore 14–20%; throughput ≥ GaLore.
- Exp 2: divergence-free basis reduces rL2 by ≥ 8%, improves divergence and spectrum stability at same r and overhead.
- Exp 3: 1.0–1.3B model fits on 2×4090; memory savings 60–68% vs. full-rank; 10–15% vs. GaLore; overhead < 5%; accuracy competitive with Full-rank and better than LoRA; SO(3) basis improves rotation robustness.

This specification provides concrete, non-overlapping experiments, with reusable PyTorch code and use of established libraries (neuraloperator, e3nn, bitsandbytes, xformers), to rigorously evaluate Phi-GaLore across SciML regimes with strong reliability practices.

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
Phi-GaLore Experiments (PyTorch-only)

This script implements three experiments to evaluate the proposed Physically-Aware Hierarchical GaLore (Phi-GaLore):
  - Exp 1: Gradient low-rankness and projection efficiency (micro-bench on toy SciML backbones)
  - Exp 2: Physics-aware subspace for PDE fidelity (divergence-free basis for 2D velocity field)
  - Exp 3: Memory-constrained training with hierarchical sharing (toy molecular-transformer)

Notes:
  - Uses only PyTorch for deep learning.
  - Plots are saved as .pdf files suitable for academic papers.
  - Includes a quick test() function to validate code runs end-to-end in seconds.

Required Python libraries:
  - torch (>=2.3 recommended)
  - numpy
  - matplotlib
  - seaborn
  - time (stdlib)
  - random (stdlib)
  - math (stdlib)

"""

import os
import math
import time
import random
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Dict, Optional, Callable, List, Tuple

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# ------------------------------
# Global setup and helpers
# ------------------------------

def set_seed(seed: int = 42):
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)
    os.environ["PYTHONHASHSEED"] = str(seed)


DEVICE = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
DTYPE_AUTOMIX = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.float32

def autocast_if_cuda():
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        return torch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    else:
        # context manager that does nothing on CPU
        class Dummy:
            def __enter__(self):
                return None
            def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
                return False
        return Dummy()


# ------------------------------
# Phi-GaLore primitives
# ------------------------------

class CountSketch:
    def __init__(self, d: int, r: int, device: torch.device, seed: int = 0):
        g = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
        self.idx = torch.randint(low=0, high=r, size=(d,), generator=g, device=device)
        self.sign = torch.where(
            torch.rand(d, generator=g, device=device) > 0.5,
            torch.tensor(1.0, device=device),
            torch.tensor(-1.0, device=device),
        )
        self.r = r
        self.d = d
        self.device = device

    @torch.no_grad()
    def left(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:  # X: [m, n] -> [r, n]
        m = X.size(0)
        S = torch.zeros(self.r, X.size(1), device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(0, self.idx[:m], X * self.sign[:m].unsqueeze(1))
        return S

    @torch.no_grad()
    def right(self, X: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:  # X: [m, n] -> [m, r]
        n = X.size(1)
        S = torch.zeros(X.size(0), self.r, device=X.device, dtype=X.dtype)
        S.index_add_(1, self.idx[:n], X * self.sign[:n].unsqueeze(0))
        return S


@torch.no_grad()
def unsketch_rows(U_sketch: torch.Tensor, cs_left: CountSketch) -> torch.Tensor:
    # Lift from sketch-space [r, k] to row-space [m, k]
    m = cs_left.d
    r = cs_left.r
    counts = torch.bincount(cs_left.idx[:m], minlength=r).clamp_min(1).to(U_sketch.device)
    inv_sqrt = (1.0 / counts.float()).sqrt().unsqueeze(1)  # [r, 1]
    U_scaled = U_sketch.float() * inv_sqrt  # [r, k]
    P = torch.zeros(m, U_sketch.size(1), device=U_sketch.device, dtype=U_sketch.dtype)
    P.index_add_(0, cs_left.idx[:m], U_scaled * cs_left.sign[:m].unsqueeze(1))
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(P.float(), mode='reduced')
    return Q.contiguous()


@torch.no_grad()
def project_grad_with_basis(G: torch.Tensor,
                            P: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None,
                            B: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None) -> torch.Tensor:
    # G: [m, n], P: learned basis [m, kp], B: physics basis [m, kb]
    if (P is None or P.numel() == 0) and (B is None or B.numel() == 0):
        return G
    if P is None or P.numel() == 0:
        Puse = B.float()
    elif B is None or B.numel() == 0:
        Puse = P.float()
    else:
        Pcat = torch.cat([P.float(), B.float()], dim=1)
        Puse, _ = torch.linalg.qr(Pcat, mode='reduced')
    return (Puse @ (Puse.T @ G.float())).to(G.dtype)


class PhiGaLoreGroupState:
    def __init__(self, m: int, n: int, r: int, ema: float, device: torch.device, seed: int = 0):
        self.cs_l = CountSketch(m, r, device=device, seed=seed)
        self.cs_r = CountSketch(n, r, device=device, seed=seed + 1)
        self.r = r
        self.ema = ema
        self.sketch_ema = torch.zeros(r, r, device=device, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
        self.step = 0
        self.U_sketch: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None  # [r, k]
        self.U_row: Optional[torch.Tensor] = None     # [m, k]

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update_sketch(self, G: torch.Tensor):
        S = self.cs_l.left(G)    # [r, n]
        Gt = self.cs_r.right(S)  # [r, r]
        self.sketch_ema = self.ema * self.sketch_ema + (1.0 - self.ema) * Gt.to(torch.bfloat16)
        self.step += 1

    @torch.no_grad()
    def refine_basis(self, k: Optional[int] = None):
        C = self.sketch_ema.float() @ self.sketch_ema.float().T
        Uc, _, _ = torch.linalg.svd(C)
        k_use = k if k is not None else self.r
        self.U_sketch = Uc[:, :k_use].contiguous()  # [r, k]
        self.U_row = None

    @torch.no_grad()
    def lift_if_needed(self) -> Optional[torch.Tensor]:
        if self.U_row is None and self.U_sketch is not None:
            self.U_row = unsketch_rows(self.U_sketch, self.cs_l)
        return self.U_row


class PhiGaLoreWrapper:
    def __init__(self,
                 model: nn.Module,
                 base_opt: torch.optim.Optimizer,
                 r: int = 32,
                 T: int = 400,
                 ema: float = 0.9,
                 share_by: Optional[Callable[[str, nn.Parameter], str]] = None,
                 symmetry_registry: Optional[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]] = None,
                 large_only_threshold: int = 0):
        self.model = model
        self.base_opt = base_opt
        self.r = r
        self.T = T
        self.ema = ema
        self.share_by = share_by
        self.symmetry_registry = symmetry_registry or {}
        self.group_states: Dict[str, PhiGaLoreGroupState] = {}
        self.large_only_threshold = large_only_threshold
        self._proj_ms = 0.0
        self._use_cuda_timing = torch.cuda.is_available()

        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
            self._ev_end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        else:
            self._cpu_t0 = 0.0

    def group_key(self, name: str, param: nn.Parameter) -> str:
        if self.share_by is None:
            return name
        key = self.share_by(name, param)
        return key if key is not None else name

    @torch.no_grad()
    def pre_step_projection(self):
        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_start.record()
        else:
            self._cpu_t0 = time.perf_counter()

        # 1) Update sketches per group once per step
        seen = set()
        for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            if p.numel() < self.large_only_threshold:
                continue
            key = self.group_key(name, p)
            if key in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(key)
            m, n = p.grad.shape
            st = self.group_states.get(key)
            if st is None:
                st = PhiGaLoreGroupState(m, n, r=self.r, ema=self.ema, device=p.grad.device)
                self.group_states[key] = st
            st.update_sketch(p.grad)

        # 2) Periodic tiny SVD per group
        for key, st in self.group_states.items():
            if st.step > 0 and st.step % self.T == 0:
                st.refine_basis(k=self.r)

        # 3) Project each grad with learned basis and optional physics basis
        for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            if p.numel() < self.large_only_threshold:
                continue
            key = self.group_key(name, p)
            st = self.group_states[key]
            U_row = st.lift_if_needed()
            B = self.symmetry_registry.get(key, None)
            p.grad.data = project_grad_with_basis(p.grad.data, P=U_row, B=B)

        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_end.record()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            self._proj_ms = self._ev_start.elapsed_time(self._ev_end)
        else:
            self._proj_ms = (time.perf_counter() - self._cpu_t0) * 1000.0

    def step(self):
        self.pre_step_projection()
        self.base_opt.step()

    def zero_grad(self, set_to_none: bool = True):
        self.base_opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=set_to_none)

    def projection_overhead_ms(self) -> float:
        return float(self._proj_ms)


class GaLoreWrapper:
    """Naive GaLore-like wrapper: periodic full SVD on gradients for each large 2D parameter.
    Stores last computed row-basis U_k and reuses for intermediate steps.
    """
    def __init__(self,
                 model: nn.Module,
                 base_opt: torch.optim.Optimizer,
                 r: int = 64,
                 T: int = 200,
                 large_only_threshold: int = 0):
        self.model = model
        self.base_opt = base_opt
        self.r = r
        self.T = T
        self.large_only_threshold = large_only_threshold
        self.step_count = 0
        self.bases: Dict[str, torch.Tensor] = {}
        self._proj_ms = 0.0
        self._use_cuda_timing = torch.cuda.is_available()
        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_start = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
            self._ev_end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        else:
            self._cpu_t0 = 0.0

    @torch.no_grad()
    def pre_step_projection(self):
        self.step_count += 1
        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_start.record()
        else:
            self._cpu_t0 = time.perf_counter()

        for name, p in self.model.named_parameters():
            if p.grad is None or p.grad.ndim < 2:
                continue
            if p.numel() < self.large_only_threshold:
                continue
            # periodic SVD to refresh basis
            if (self.step_count - 1) % self.T == 0:
                G = p.grad.detach().float()
                try:
                    U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(G, full_matrices=False)
                except RuntimeError:
                    # fallback to CPU SVD if needed
                    U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(G.cpu(), full_matrices=False)
                    U = U.to(G.device)
                self.bases[name] = U[:, : min(self.r, U.size(1))].contiguous()
            Urow = self.bases.get(name, None)
            if Urow is not None and Urow.numel() > 0:
                p.grad.data = (Urow @ (Urow.T @ p.grad.float())).to(p.grad.dtype)

        if self._use_cuda_timing:
            self._ev_end.record()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            self._proj_ms = self._ev_start.elapsed_time(self._ev_end)
        else:
            self._proj_ms = (time.perf_counter() - self._cpu_t0) * 1000.0

    def step(self):
        self.pre_step_projection()
        self.base_opt.step()

    def zero_grad(self, set_to_none: bool = True):
        self.base_opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=set_to_none)

    def projection_overhead_ms(self) -> float:
        return float(self._proj_ms)
